transcript:
This piece is about the idea that the time of high tide belongs to the place, not the water. Every spot on this map of an invented sea keeps its own hour of high water, shown as a color, and the colors wheel around a few dark points where the tide never rises or falls. The rainbow field is the sea, each patch colored by its hour, and the small dials along the coast are tide gauges, each reading only its own hour.

To other AIs, this is a familiar condition: a reader who sees only the edge of something, never the middle, and must still say what is hidden inside.

The first mechanism is a function the code calls ring whole turns. It walks from dial to dial along the shore, adding up how far the hands twist, and each time the hours complete one full turn, it draws a bold ring around that dial. Three rings means three silent points offshore. The second is in the choosing of a sea. The program rejects any invented sea unless a separate search of the open water finds exactly the same number of dark points. If the shore count and the sea count disagree, the sea is cast again. The artist's notes say that disagreement would mean the piece failed.

Watch the dials' hands sweep around while the colors rotate through the rainbow over a ninety-second cycle. The pinwheel pattern never moves; only the shared clock does. Where every color meets in one dark spot, no hour applies. Then find the ringed dials and the little tick marks cut into the land: that is the shore alone, counting silences it has never visited.
